en: Uncle, I shall die by your hand,
I shall not let you go unless I die.
If I do not see your true resting place,
If I do not die together with you,
If I do not hew off his head with an axe,
If I do not cut through his neck with a sword,
If I do not see the face of the world beyond,
If I do not die locked in your embrace,
May I die unworthy of the name Külchoro,
Let me see whether you will speak.
Just utter something by chance,
And I shall take it as a sign.
If you will not speak to me,
If you will not heed what I say,
I shall disfigure you now,
I shall unleash my towering rage.
I said I had fallen into the embers for you,
I was scorched and became an ember myself.
I burned and burned until I was gone,
I wore out my heroic head,
I aged my strongman's soul.
I was blinded and became as a grave,
I became level with the black earth.
Every ordeal and mighty torment,
I was the one who endured it all.
For you, bloodthirsty villain of the dark day,
Only a spoonful of my blood remains,
My flesh is left bruised and raw,
I fell from my course and was left bereft.
When the mighty gray-maned hero was lost,
They said, “The valiant man has seen
The true abode from which none return,”
They would wash him with koumiss,
And wrap him in brocade,
They would wash him with Zamzam water,
And bind him in cloth of gold,
Entrust him to the wise for safekeeping,
And have singers praise him,
Entrust him to men of honor,
And have poets sing his praise.
If I do not bury him with my own hands,
May I die unworthy of the name Külchoro,
May I sink into darkness as though never born.
Turn your neck toward me,
Uncle, while you are still alive,
Reveal your inmost secret.
The song you spoke in truth,
Speak it sincerely as your creed.
Tell me the secret within you,
Tell me the truth.
When spears are gripped and ranks broken,
And doomed men fly before bullets,
When the great turmoil arose,
What calamity did you wrap yourself in,
What affliction befell you,
Uncle, driven from your people,
What ordeal overtook you?
I have burned and smoldered in anguish,
Long ago I lost all hope,
Then I encountered you on the open steppe,
And found you again for myself.
You turned affliction into a grievous disease,
And renewed my sorrow once more.
Your upland dwelling was a white palace,
Yet I endured much of your hell.
I suffered servitude of every kind,
For food I took blows upon my knuckles,
All the while calling you my princely uncle.
And now, meeting you upon the road,
Finding you on the open steppe,
You sought to chill my breath.
You sought to knock the wind from me,
You sought to break my back.
You would not listen to my words,
You made me, the gray-maned hero, waste away.
Now, sultan, hear my words!
In earnest I shall spill my blood,
In truth I shall sacrifice my life.
You knocked the swelling wind from me,
You truly chilled my breath.
If you remain silent without a word,
And persist in such stubbornness,
If I do not cleave your head with my sword,
If I do not die right before you,
May I die without another soul being born,
You turned my burning soul into an ember,
I shall quarrel with you once
And see what comes of it.
Let us bind on keen red spears,
And wage fiercer war than against the Chinese,
Let us bind on keen black spears,
And fight like mortal enemies,
Thrusting spears at one another,
Spilling blood like water,
And smashing our stout ribs
And vertebrae with cracking blows.
If I do not fight you and see,
If I let you go without dying,
May I die unworthy of the name Külchoro,
Let me meet the death I have awaited
Head-on before you,
You valiant, bloodthirsty tiger.
My wrath has risen and I stand rigid,
Let me grapple with you and see,
If my mortal doom comes today,
I shall meet it face-to-face.
The ultimate, utter catastrophe
I shall bring upon you, noble lord.
If I do not find a way to overcome you now,
If I do not find it by swinging my sharp blade,
Then I have been sold as a black slave.
I wandered gathering firewood,
Until the flesh of my soles was blistered,
My strength departed and I became blind,
My head grew crazed with grief.
Long did I live in servitude,
Wondering whence the tiger of the walled city
Could ever come.
Now I have seen you alive with my own eyes,
Though I needlessly let myself waste away.
You made me roam as a helpless wretch,
Without speaking a word or uttering a sound.
Why have you tormented me so much?
You drained away my strength,
Why did you set my soul aflame,
Why did you make my blood boil so often?
When I clung to you in hope,
Why did you crush my soul?
You ruined my blooming countenance,
Why did you provoke my rage?
For many days you made me endure
The bitter day I see today.
When I turned to you, you ignored my words,
Though we were kin who never turned away—
Could you not at least look me in the eye?
Alas, my uncle, sultan and lion!
May our father be your sacrifice,
O luckless hero dearer than a father,
Without a word you made me cry out,
Why did you make me lament so?
Our sheep shared the same fold,
Our food the same fellowship,
Whatever we found, we gathered together,
We shared death and shared the faith.
Our grazing herds and encampment were one,
Our lives and our common death were one.
When we entered battle, we shared its dust,
Our lives and destined death were one,
Though I pleaded and stared imploringly,
You stared in confusion like a mute.
His bearing was proud, his eyes deep black,
Tall in stature and broad of shoulder,
Both strongman and lionhearted hero,
A luckless hero capable of making
The whole world submit.
He looked from side to side,
Licking his lips,
Roaring in anger,
Shouting fearsomely.
His redness was like dun-colored fur,
And if you heard his cry,
It was like a lion's roar.
His eyes were like embers of saxaul,
When his gray mane crackled,
It was like a bolt of lightning,
Such was the sight of his power.
His giant frame was like a lion,
No soul could withstand his terror,
But panicked, unable to find a way out.
He seemed to swoop upon whomever he met,
And bear them off like a giant bird,
Fearing nothing beneath the moon and sky;
Allah Most High indeed creates
His servants in every form,
And such was Külchoro's form.
The space between his shoulders
Was like a field sown with grain;
Would anyone who challenged
That wrathful gray-maned hero remain alive?
The corners of his eyes were like flint,
As though this gray-maned hero could swallow the world
At the mere sound of his name.
If you looked at his ears,
The poor man bore the mark of a fortress,
As though he sucked out men's souls in combat.
His wildness was like a boar's,
His crackling like dry straw,
And a rash enemy who fought him
Could neither measure nor master his strength.
His charge was like a whirlwind.
I am dead, not alive,
Yet instead of dying I became an ember,
Living on as I waited for you.
Appearing alive, you made me rejoice,
Only to burn and scorch me utterly.
Vanishing beyond sight,
You abandoned livestock and household without a guardian.
When I catch hold of you, you say nothing;
Why did you begin acting like a helpless wretch?
For pity's sake, uncle, speak—
What my eyes saw from the ridge!
Would it not have been far better
Had you died instead of living?
Exalting your lionhearted pride,
You conceal your words without speaking,
You have knocked the wind from me,
You have quenched and chilled my breath.
Tell me your words, uncle;
If you stand there suddenly
Without speaking or uttering a sound,
And my wrath rises till I stand rigid,
A mighty quarrel will suddenly erupt.
The mystic's cave will turn to dust,
The face of the earth will run red with blood.
If I roar out in anger,
Those I encounter will lie dead,
So take care, lest I spring suddenly.
I may pounce upon you without warning!”
So spoke Külchoro,
His lionlike nature showing,
His furious rage pouring out.
His beard was like a quiver case,
His upright mustache
Like the haft of a greasy axe;
Such was Choro when you saw him.
He looked every bit the hero one could desire;
When wrath made him stand rigid,
He seemed ready to devour whoever challenged him,
Such was Külchoro's nature.
Broad-chested, with a spacious breast,
Such was Külchoro's nature,
His bloodlust seized him.
Power surged from his imposing frame,
And from the fire of his two cheeks
Sprang enough hair to fill a stocking.
Whenever Külchoro grew impassioned,
He would take his spear in his right hand,
And when wrath made him stand rigid,
He would bring slaughter upon the world.
When he truly gripped its shaft,
When the lone champion took it in hand,
He would scout the road alone,
Rout Jeti-Kait and seize its spoils.
If an enemy boasted of strength,
He shook down the mightiest.
He drove strongmen into flight,
And when an enemy came to grapple,
He drove his black-steel spear
Deep between his ribs.
When Semetey's cause fell to him,
Elkindi became his mountain encampment.
He made the whole world submit,
A lionhearted hero who spared himself nothing.
He flashed like a bird of prey,
Cracked like a white musket,
And spoke without holding back.
